utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, please. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-97-24-I, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus others and Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say good afternoon to the interpreters and to the audio-visual booth and be sure that everybody can hear me. Thank you. And I would like to say good afternoon to the public who has come to witness this hearing. These are part of the preliminary hearings, that is, the initial appearance of the accused, which is covered by Rule 62 of our rules. Let me now turn to the Prosecutor, Ms. Susan Somers. Would you please tell us who is representing the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the Prosecution team, Susan Somers. Also present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise. For the Prosecution team, Susan Somers. Also with the Prosecution, Daniel Saxon, Kapila Waidyaratne, and Ms. Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me thank you very much. Let me now turn to the Defence, although we know one another, Mr. Lukic. Would you please introduce yourself, to say the bar you represent, and what your qualifications are at the Tribunal. In any case, as you have presented them to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you for giving me the floor. I am Branko Lukic, lawyer from Doboj, Republika Srpska, BNH, and I have master degree in law. Today I am representing Mr. Milomir Stakic only on this initial appearance. I suggested to Mr. Stakic to find a permanent lawyer as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Lukic. You may be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to turn now to Mr. Milomir Stakic who is appearing today for the first time further to an indictment which was prepared against him. Mr. Stakic, would you please rise. Would you clearly state your name and your first name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date and place of your birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19th of January, 1962, in Maricka in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession, please, and what is your residence, the residence you occupied before coming here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a doctor, a general practitioner, currently undergoing specialisation, my residency for physical therapy until my arrival here in The Hague. That was what I have been doing. I did my residency in Belgrade in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you have children?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Dr. Stakic. This is your Initial Appearance before the Tribunal. Of course, it is a significant formality, but you must be present and conscious, with your attorney, of what is going on, because this is the time since your arrest when you are once again given the opportunity to familiarise yourself with all of the charges which the Prosecutor has brought against you and which were confirmed by a Judge, until such time as evidence is presented in a adversarial proceeding. For things to be clear, Dr. Stakic, I am going to ask first the registrar to refer to the constituent text which give to you several rights and which will then allow you to move to the most important part of this appearance, that is, to ask you whether you wish to plead guilty or not guilty, and to know that if you plead guilty or not guilty, the Court will know. For the time being, please be seated, Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Stakic, please pay careful attention to the reading out of this text. I can say this to your counsel as well, but of course I'm sure that your counsel is very familiar with it. Madam Registrar, would you please read out the Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute, and 62 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. SENIOR LEGAL OFFICER: [Interpretation] Mr. President, excuse me. Perhaps the reading could be done in French. That would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please proceed. SENIOR LEGAL OFFICER: [Interpretation] Article 20 of the Tribunal, Commencement of Trial Proceedings:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 1. The Trial Chambers shall ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, with full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses. 2. A person against whom an indictment has been confirmed shall, pursuant to an order or an arrest warrant of the International Tribunal, to be taken into custody, immediately informed of the charges against him and transferred to the International Tribunal. 3. A trial should not commence until the accused is physically present before the International Tribunal and the indictment is read out, and to be sure that the rights of the accused are to be respected, confirms that the accused has understood the contents of the indictment and orders him to plead guilty or not guilty. The Chamber then sets the date for the trial. 4. The hearings shall be public unless the Trial Chamber decides to close the proceedings in accordance with its Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Article 21, The Rights of the Accused:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 1. All persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal. 2. In the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing, subject to Article 22 of the Statute. 3. The accused shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to the provisions of the present Statute. 4. In the determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees, in full equality: (a) to be informed promptly and in detail, in a language which he understands, of the nature and cause of the charge against him; (b) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing; (c) to be tried without undue delay; (d) to be tried in his presence and to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing; to be informed, if he does not have legal assistance, of this right; and to have legal assistance assigned to him, in any case where the interests of justice so require, and without payment by him in any such case if he does not have sufficient means to pay for it; (e) to examine, or have examined, the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him; (f) to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in the International Tribunal; (g) not to be compelled to testify himself or to confess guilt. Rule 62 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, Initial Appearance of the accused:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Upon transfer of an accused to the seat of the Tribunal, the President shall forthwith assign the case to a Trial Chamber. The accused shall be brought before that Trial Chamber or a Judge thereof without delay and shall be formally charged. The Trial Chamber or the Judge shall 1) satisfy himself or herself of the right of the accused to counsel is respected; 2) to have or have the indictment read to the accused in a language the accused speaks and understands, and satisfy itself, himself or herself, that the accused understands the indictment. Inform the accused that within 30 days of his initial appearance, he or she will be called upon to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count, but that should the accused so request, he or she may immediately enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on one or more counts. If the accused fails to enter a plea at the initial or any further appearance, enter a plea of not guilty on the accused's behalf. In case of a plea of not guilty, instruct the registrar to set a date for trial. In case of a plea of guilty, if before the Trial Chamber, act in accordance with Rule 62 bis; or, if before a Judge, refer the plea to the Trial Chamber so that it may act in accordance with Rule 62 bis. Instruct the registrar to assess such other dates as appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Olivier Fourmy for having read out these texts. Let me now turn to Mr. Branko Lukic. Has Dr. Stakic received a copy of the indictment in a language which -- in his own language, and has he understood its contents? Would you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He received the indictment, and he received it in the language he understands, and he read it thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you able to speak with Dr. Stakic about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We had a lengthy discussion, and we discussed the whole indictment in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Stakic, would you rise, please. Have you received the indictment in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you understood its content?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you prepared today to tell us whether you plead guilty or not guilty to the counts?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am prepared to enter my plea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that everything is clear, Dr. Stakic, we are going to proceed as follows: The registrar is going to read out the indictment. You will remain seated while she reads it, and when we reach the count, I'm going to ask you to rise and I will ask you whether you plead guilty or not guilty. Have you understood what I've said, and do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, you may be seated. Mr. Lukic, I would like to know whether you agree to our reading only part of the indictment, that is, paragraphs 3, 10 to 12, and 19 to 26. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are ready even to waive our right to have the indictment read, but we leave it to the Chamber to decide how to deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic, for having cooperated with us, but the Trial Chamber nonetheless believes that in respect of information for the public, some information should be given, and so the Chamber orders that the relevant paragraphs be read out, that is, paragraphs 3, 10 to 12, and then 19 to 26. Madam Registrar, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Paragraph 3: Milomir Stakic was born on 19th February 1962 in the municipality of Prijedor of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1992, he served as the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor municipality and as a member of the municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff. He is a doctor of profession and is currently serving again as president of the municipality of Prijedor. Paragraph 10: During the period from 29th of April, 1992, to the 31st of December, 1992, Milomir Stakic was both a member of the municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff and the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. In his role as a member of the Crisis Staff, Milomir Stakic was part of the body that held executive power in the municipality of Prijedor at all times relevant to this indictment and the body referred to in paragraph 5 above. As the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, Milomir Stakic occupied the most important position on the Crisis Staff in terms of the de jure authority. He had the final voice and authority in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deciding all issues within the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stakic, excuse me, would you please rise. Continue, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 1: Genocide. Between 19 -- April 1992 and January 1993, others and Milomir Stakic did, in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by their acts and omissions, commit genocide. Beginning in the spring of 1992, the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, including others and Milomir Stakic, planned, organised and implemented the creation of a number of detention facilities or camps, including the Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje camps. These camps were staffed and operated by military and police personnel and their agents, under the control of the Bosnian Serb military and civilian members of the Crisis Staff. In addition, other Bosnian Serb police, military, and civilians not directly assigned to the guard staff of the camps had unfettered access to all of the detention facilities and operated in conjunction with the personnel in control of these detention facilities. In none of the camps were the detainees afforded proper judicial process and their internment was not justified by military necessity. They were detained primarily because of their religious and ethnic identification. The conditions in the Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje camps were abject and brutal. Bosnian Serb military and police personnel in charge of these facilities, their staff, and other persons who visited the camps, all of whom were subject to the authority and control of the Crisis Staff, killed, sexually assaulted, tortured, and otherwise physically and psychologically abused the detainees in the camps. At Omarska and Keraterm, the camps were deliberately operated in a manner designed to inflict upon the detainees conditions intended to bring about their physical destruction with the intent to destroy, in part, the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat people as national, ethnic, or religious groups. Serious violations of international humanitarian law of a similar pattern were committed in both Omarska and Keraterm camps. Detainees were continuously subjected to or forced to witness inhumane acts, including murder, rape, sexual assault, torture, beatings and robbery, as well as other forms of mental and physical abuse. Daily food rations provided to detainees amounted to starvation rations. Medical care for the detainees was insufficient or non-existent, and the general hygienic conditions prevalent at these camps were grossly inadequate. At Omarska, prisoners were crowded together with little or no facilities for personal hygiene. They were fed starvation rations once a day and given only a few minutes to go to the canteen area, eat and then leave. The little water they received was often foul. Prisoners had no changes of clothing and no bedding. They received no medical care. Killings and severe beatings of prisoners were commonplace. The camp guards, who were both police and military personnel, and others who came to the camp and physically abused the prisoners, used all manner of weapons during these beatings, including wooden batons, metal rods and tools, lengths of thick industrial cable, rifle butts and knives. Both female and male prisoners were beaten, raped, sexually assaulted, tortured and humiliated. Hundreds of the detainees, whose identities are known and unknown, did not survive the camp. Keraterm camp was located the a former ceramics factory in Prijedor. Conditions for prisoners were similar to those in Omarska camp. Detainees were so crowded in the four rooms that, on many occasions, they could not lie down. The detainees were not permitted to move around freely in the camp. Whether detained in the rooms or on the open area outside, they were only allowed to move when specifically permitted to do so, usually only to receive their starvation rations or to go to the toilet. On a daily basis, the camp leadership, the camp guards, who were both police and military personnel, and others who came to the camp to abuse the detainees, subjected the detainees to inhuman conditions, physical violence, constant humiliation, degradation, and fear of death. Many detainees were executed in the camp. On one night in July 1992, more than 150 military-aged men from the Brdo region were executed. Severe beatings were commonplace. All manner of weapons were used during these beatings, including wooden batons, metal rods, baseball bats, lengths of thick industrial cable, rifle butts and knives. The beatings, sexual assaults, tortures and other cruel and humiliating actions were generally inflicted in full view of other detainees and were accompanied by derogatory and humiliating comments to the victims or their families and general threats to the other detainees. After they were beaten, tortured, or sexually assaulted, the detainees were carried, dragged, or forced to crawl back into their rooms, without any form of care for their injuries. Hundreds of detainees, whose identities are known and unknown, did not survive the camp. Trnopolje camp was established at the site of a former school and adjacent buildings in Trnopolje village. It was the largest camp and the location to which Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat women, children, and elderly were taken. Some men of military age also managed to go directly to the Trnopolje camp. The buildings in the camp were quickly filled and the remaining detainees had to find shelter in makeshift huts of plastic and excess materials or remain out in the open fields. The hygiene facilities were grossly inadequate. Minimal rations were provided on a sporadic basis, with female detainees eventually being allowed to leave the camp to forage for food in the surrounding village. The camp served as the staging point for the mass deportation of all those who survived the initial attacks and camp regime. It also served a much more sinister purpose: the sexual assault, rape, and torture of many of the women detained there by camp personnel, who were both police and military personnel, and by other military units from the area who came to the camp for that specific purpose. In many instances, the women and girls were taken from the camp and raped, tortured, or sexually abused at other locations. In addition, many prisoners, both male and female, were killed, beaten, and otherwise physically and psychologically maltreated by the camp personnel and other Serbs and Bosnian Serbs who were allowed into the camp. Between 30 April 1992 and 31 December 1992, others and Milomir Stakic, in concert with others, planned, instigated, and ordered the establishment of the camps at Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje and the detention therein of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the municipality of Prijedor under conditions calculated to bring about the physical destruction of the detainees, with the intent to destroy part of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat groups, as such. Further, between 30 April 1992 and 31 December 1992, others and Milomir Stakic knew or had reason to know that their subordinates who staffed the detention facilities were killing or causing serious physical or mental harm to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats with the intent to destroy them, in part, as a national, ethnic, or religious group, or had done so and failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. By these acts and omissions, others and Milomir Stakic were complicit in the commission of genocide, punishable under Articles 4(3)(e) and 7(1) and (3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Dr. Stakic, do you plead guilty or do you plead not guilty to the single count of genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plead not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have taken note that Dr. Stakic has pleaded not guilty to the count of genocide. Madam Registrar, please note that Dr. Stakic has pleaded not guilty to the count. Mr. Lukic, and for the Prosecutor as well, I'd like to provide a small explanation. The Chamber has decided to replace the name of Simo Drljaca and Milan Kovacevic by the word "others" because, as you know, those individuals are deceased, and therefore we are saying "others." I'm only saying this so that things be clear. Dr. Stakic, you may be seated. We must now anticipate how we're going to organise the case. There are two preliminary questions which I would like to ask the Prosecutor so that we be aware of what it is that we are speaking of. I don't know if you are in a position, Ms. Somers, to answer the question. Does the Prosecutor wish to amend the indictment, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution indeed will be amending the indictment and has undertaken steps to do so already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, Ms. Somers: Can you tell us why the Prosecutor did not do that when the indictment was amended in respect of the other person, Milan Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Having inquired into some of the history of the amendments with co-defendants, it appears that decisions to wait until apprehension were made. In part, the Prosecution has an obligation at the time of arrest to review the state of the evidence, indeed, and amendment is most common, having made such a review. It is also imperative to review the state of jurisprudence that has changed since 1997. And having taken these factors into account upon the arrest of the accused Stakic, we have undertaken to make the necessary amendments and we'll file according to Rule 50 in due course. I have indicated this to Mr. Lukic prior to the session commencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Somers. Do you have any idea as to when you are going to present an amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It would be difficult to give an exact date to be held to. I can indicate to the Chamber that work has already been undertaken in that direction, and given the various time limits that we have in terms of other Rules being triggered, we will do so as speedily as possible and we will keep whatever Defence counsel is assigned current on the state of things. I have also spoken, if I may indicate to the Chamber, with Mr. Lukic about the normal documents which would accompany the appearance. Because we have discussed, first of all, that Mr. Lukic is making only a temporary appearance, it appears, at this time, he has indicated to me, and perhaps the Chamber will inquire directly of him, that he would not wish to accept now the documents which would go with the 1997 indictment, but rather, when permanent counsel is assigned, to make the determination or have that individual make the determination. Further, if other materials for the new indictment, in fact, assuming it has been already confirmed, are available, that may alter the timing of the delivery. I do wish to indicate, however, that the Prosecution is, with due diligence, working on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in any case, Ms. Somers, in respect of Rule 66 of the Rules, that you in some way have just mentioned, is the Prosecutor prepared to transmit the documents which accompanied the confirmation to a counsel as soon as that counsel is appointed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, the Prosecution has today the documents that were accompanying that particular indictment. All but 19 have been translated into English. Nineteen pages, excuse me. Nineteen pages, not nineteen documents. And therefore, as soon as said counsel is appointed, we are prepared, certainly, to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will wait until the registry assigns counsel, Dr. Stakic. And we want the registrar to tell us when the date of that assignment will be so we can set up a Status Conference to see where we stand. And I would also tell you that the Trial Chamber is going to appoint a Pre-Trial Judge, and at the appropriate time it will inform you of who that person is. I think there are no further issues to be dealt with. Mr. Lukic, are there any other things you would like to raise now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, we don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now turn to Dr. Stakic. Would you rise, please. I'm going to give you the floor so that you can speak about your medical condition and your detention conditions and to tell us whether there are any other statements that you would like to make right now. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this time, Your Honour, I do not have any statements to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may be seated, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, we will inform you of the date of the Status Conference and we will wait until the Registry tells us when the counsel will be assigned. For the time being, there are no further issues to deal with. I adjourn the Court and I wish you a pleasant afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.45 p.m.
